To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) a small-world NoC architecture with long-range wireless connections can provide a significant energy and performance advantage over a conventional NoC, and (b) the energy efficiency of the small-world NoC is further improved by using a novel wireless link design that is capable of dynamically adjusting its transmission range.

(1) a small-world topology with on-chip long-range wireless links can be designed with a low area overhead; (2) the wireless links can be used to implement a low-power and energy efficient NoC architecture; (3) the wireless links are able to provide a low latency and a high bandwidth; (4) the wireless links enable a sustainable multi-core architecture that can operate with a low power consumption, a low chip temperature, and a high performance.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that small-world NoCs can be implemented with wireless links and that such a NoC architecture can achieve high performance and energy efficiency.
we have demonstrated that wireless links are a promising solution for energy efficient NoC architectures.
we have developed a new paradigm in which the NoC architecture itself is the key component in the energy-efficient design of multi-core chips.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the wireless interconnects enable a significant reduction in the energy consumed for communication, which in turn allows for an increase in the number of cores that can be supported on a single chip, and thus a higher performance per watt.

the combination of small-world topology with wireless NoC can be used to significantly reduce energy consumption, while maintaining high performance, and thus enabling the design of sustainable high-performance multi-core systems.
the wireless links can be used to reduce the power and thermal constraints on the NoC architecture and thus enable more efficient use of the available chip resources.
